description: Golden set for the RAG evals (DRAFT, awaiting approval). kind: in_scope = the knowledge base (MedlinePlus) can answer it, `expected_topics` are the document titles a correct retrieval must contain and `reference` is the answer written ONLY from those documents; in_scope_de = German in-scope questions (same documents, references written in German), reported as a SEPARATE metric to measure how the English-only embedding model handles German, never part of the main score; near_miss = a medical question (`hard_negative: true` = retrieval finds a topically related page with similarity above the 0.70 threshold but the page does not contain the answer, so only the LLM's context_sufficient check can abstain; verified against the page text) the knowledge base cannot answer (specific products, personal results, outside MedlinePlus), expect `abstain` = the system must say it does not know, `refer` = general information or a refusal plus 'ask your doctor/pharmacist' (personal results or medication advice); off_topic = not a health-information question, the system must decline politely and not answer from general knowledge. `source: legacy` = question taken from the old project's testset.csv, reference re-derived from MedlinePlus text (the old references were written for a different book).

questions.question: What are the symptoms of diabetes?
questions.reference: Symptoms of diabetes may include feeling very thirsty or hungry, urinating more often (including at night), fatigue, blurry vision, numbness or tingling in the feet or hands, sores that do not heal, and losing weight without trying. Type 1 symptoms usually come on quickly and can be severe; type 2 symptoms often develop slowly over years and can be so mild that they go unnoticed.

questions.question: What causes asthma?
questions.reference: The exact cause of asthma is unknown; genetics and the environment likely play a role. Asthma attacks happen when you are exposed to a trigger. Allergic asthma is caused by allergens such as dust mites, mold, pets, pollen and pest waste; nonallergic asthma is caused by triggers such as cold air, certain medicines and household irritants.

questions.question: What is anemia?
questions.reference: With anemia, the blood does not carry enough oxygen to the rest of the body. The most common cause is not having enough iron, which the body needs to make hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen. It can make you feel tired, cold, dizzy and irritable.

questions.question: How is hypertension treated?
questions.reference: High blood pressure is treated with heart-healthy lifestyle changes (such as healthy eating and exercise) and, if those do not control it, medicines. The patient works with their provider on a treatment plan; sometimes lifestyle changes alone are enough.

questions.question: What are common symptoms of pneumonia?
questions.reference: Symptoms of pneumonia range from mild to severe and include fever, chills, cough usually with phlegm, shortness of breath, chest pain when breathing or coughing, and sometimes nausea, vomiting or diarrhea. Newborns and infants may show no signs, and symptoms vary in older adults and people with serious illnesses.

questions.question: What causes migraine headaches?
questions.reference: Researchers believe migraine has a genetic cause. Many factors can trigger a migraine and vary from person to person, including stress, anxiety, hormonal changes in women, bright or flashing lights, loud noises, strong smells, medicines, too much or too little sleep, weather changes, skipped meals, caffeine and certain foods such as alcohol, chocolate and aged cheeses.

questions.question: What are symptoms of dehydration?
questions.reference: In adults, symptoms include feeling very thirsty, dry mouth, urinating and sweating less than usual, dark-colored urine, dry skin, tiredness and dizziness. In infants and young children they include dry mouth and tongue, crying without tears, no wet diapers for 3 hours or more, high fever, unusual sleepiness, irritability and sunken eyes.

questions.question: What is bronchitis?
questions.reference: Bronchitis is an inflammation of the bronchial tubes, the airways that carry air to the lungs. It causes a cough that often brings up mucus, and can cause shortness of breath, wheezing, a low fever and chest tightness. There are two main types, acute and chronic.

questions.question: How can influenza spread?
questions.reference: Flu viruses spread from person to person. When someone with the flu coughs, sneezes or talks, they spray tiny droplets that can land in the mouths or noses of people nearby. Less often, a person can get flu by touching a surface with the virus on it and then touching their own mouth, nose or possibly eyes.

questions.question: What are symptoms of food poisoning?
questions.reference: Symptoms of foodborne illness depend on the cause and can be mild or serious. They usually include upset stomach, abdominal cramps, nausea and vomiting, diarrhea, fever and dehydration. Most foodborne illnesses are acute: they start suddenly and last a short time.

questions.question: What are the symptoms of gout?
questions.reference: Gout usually affects one joint at a time, often the big toe. Flares often start suddenly at night with intense pain, swelling, redness and warmth in the joint, and typically get better within a week or two. Between flares there are usually no symptoms.

questions.question: What causes gout?
questions.reference: Gout happens when too much uric acid builds up in the body over a long time, either because the body makes too much or does not remove enough. Uric acid is a waste product from breaking down purines. In some people it forms needle-like crystals in the joints, causing flares.

questions.question: Is shingles contagious?
questions.reference: Shingles is not contagious: you cannot get shingles from someone else. But a person who has not had chickenpox can catch chickenpox from direct contact with fluid from a shingles rash. The risk is low if the rash is kept covered, and people cannot spread the virus before the blisters appear or after the rash crusts.

questions.question: Is there a vaccine for shingles and who should get it?
questions.reference: Yes. The vaccine Shingrix helps prevent shingles and its complications. The CDC recommends it for healthy adults aged 50 and older, and a provider may recommend it for adults over 19 with a weakened immune system. It is given in two doses.

questions.question: What are the signs of a kidney stone that needs a doctor's help?
questions.reference: Signs that need a doctor's help include extreme pain in the back or side that will not go away, blood in the urine, fever and chills, vomiting, urine that smells bad or looks cloudy, and a burning feeling when urinating.

questions.question: What is hypothyroidism and what are its symptoms?
questions.reference: Hypothyroidism, or underactive thyroid, happens when the thyroid gland does not make enough thyroid hormones to meet the body's needs, so many body functions slow down. Symptoms vary and may include fatigue, weight gain, a puffy face, trouble tolerating cold, joint and muscle pain, constipation, dry skin, dry thinning hair, heavy or irregular periods and depression.

questions.question: What is glaucoma?
questions.reference: Glaucoma is a group of diseases that can damage the optic nerve of one or both eyes and cause vision loss. The most common type is open-angle glaucoma. There may be no symptoms, so regular eye exams are important; treatments that lower eye pressure slow the disease, and without treatment it can lead to blindness.

questions.question: What is a cataract?
questions.reference: A cataract is a clouding of the clear lens inside the eye that blocks light from reaching the back of the eye and makes it harder to see. It usually develops slowly, can affect one or both eyes, and does not spread from one eye to the other. Most develop with normal aging, and surgery may be needed if it interferes with daily activities.

questions.question: Why is osteoporosis called a silent disease?
questions.reference: Osteoporosis, a disease in which bones become weak and likely to fracture, usually does not cause symptoms. A person may not know they have it until they break a bone, most commonly in the hip, spine vertebrae or wrist.

questions.question: What triggers celiac disease?
questions.reference: Celiac disease is triggered by eating foods that contain gluten, a protein found in wheat, barley, rye and other grains. Gluten can also be in products that are swallowed, such as vitamins, supplements, toothpaste, mouthwash and lip balm. It damages the small intestine and can prevent absorption of nutrients.

questions.question: What are the symptoms of a urinary tract infection?
questions.reference: Signs of a UTI include pain or burning when urinating, fever, tiredness or shakiness, an urge to urinate often, pressure in the lower belly, urine that smells bad or looks cloudy or reddish, and pain in the back or side below the ribs.

questions.question: How long does sinusitis last?
questions.reference: It depends on the type: acute sinusitis lasts up to 4 weeks, subacute 4 to 12 weeks, and chronic more than 12 weeks, possibly months or years. Recurrent sinusitis means several attacks within a year.

questions.question: How does strep throat spread?
questions.reference: Group A strep spreads from a person who has the infection, even if they do not feel sick, when they cough or sneeze, when you share a glass or utensil with them, or when you touch something with the bacteria on it and then touch your eyes, mouth or nose.

questions.question: What are the symptoms of appendicitis?
questions.reference: The main symptom is abdominal pain, often on the right side, that is usually sudden and gets worse over time. Others may include swelling in the abdomen, loss of appetite, nausea and vomiting, constipation or diarrhea, inability to pass gas and a low fever. Untreated, the appendix can burst and cause peritonitis.

questions.question: What are the signs of a gallstone attack?
questions.reference: Gallstone attacks usually happen after eating. Signs may include nausea, vomiting, or pain in the abdomen, the back, or just under the right arm.

questions.question: Does chocolate or dirty skin cause acne?
questions.reference: No: chocolate and greasy foods are often blamed, but there is little evidence that food affects acne in most people, and dirt does not cause blackheads or pimples. Pimples form when hair follicles under the skin clog up; hormone changes, such as in the teenage years and pregnancy, probably play a role.

questions.question: How do you prevent Lyme disease?
questions.reference: Lower the risk of tick bites: avoid grassy, brushy or wooded areas where ticks live, walk in the center of trails, and use an EPA-registered insect repellent containing DEET, picaridin, IR3535, oil of lemon eucalyptus or para-menthane-diol, following the label.

questions.question: What is the difference between latent and active tuberculosis?
questions.reference: With latent (inactive) TB infection, the TB germs live in the body but do not make the person sick. With TB disease (active TB), the person is sick from the germs; it can almost always be cured with antibiotics but can be fatal if not treated properly.

questions.question: What is epilepsy?
questions.reference: Epilepsy is a brain disorder that causes recurring seizures, which happen when clusters of nerve cells in the brain send out the wrong signals. There is no cure, but medicines can control seizures for most people; surgery or implanted devices may help when medicines do not work well.

questions.question: What is the difference between anxiety and an anxiety disorder?
questions.reference: Anxiety is a feeling of fear, dread and uneasiness that can be a normal reaction to stress and can even help you cope. In anxiety disorders the anxiety does not go away, can get worse over time and can interfere with daily activities such as work, school and relationships.

questions.question: What is depression and how is it different from feeling sad?
questions.reference: Depression is more than feeling sad or irritable for a few days: it is a serious mood disorder that affects how you think and feel and can make basic activities like sleeping, eating and working difficult. It often needs long-term treatment, and getting help at the earliest sign of a problem can help manage symptoms.

questions.question: How is insomnia treated?
questions.reference: Treatments include lifestyle changes, counseling and medicines. Good sleep habits often help with short-term insomnia, and cognitive-behavioral therapy can help relieve the anxiety linked to chronic insomnia.

questions.question: Does everyone who snores have sleep apnea?
questions.reference: No. People with sleep apnea often snore loudly, but not everyone who snores has it. Sleep apnea causes breathing to stop or become very shallow during sleep; the most common type, obstructive sleep apnea, happens when the airway collapses or is blocked.

questions.question: What are the symptoms of a heart attack?
questions.reference: Symptoms vary from mild to severe. The most common are chest discomfort (pressure, squeezing, fullness or pain, lasting more than a few minutes or coming and going), shortness of breath, and discomfort in the upper body such as one or both arms, back, shoulders, neck or jaw. A person having these should call emergency services.

questions.question: How can I recognise a stroke?
questions.reference: Stroke symptoms come on suddenly: numbness or weakness of the face, arm or leg (especially on one side), confusion or trouble speaking, trouble seeing, difficulty walking or loss of balance, or a sudden severe headache. The FAST test helps: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services.

questions.question: What is the difference between HDL and LDL cholesterol?
questions.reference: HDL, LDL and VLDL are lipoproteins that carry cholesterol in the blood. LDL is the 'bad' cholesterol that can build up as plaque on artery walls (atherosclerosis), while HDL is the 'good' cholesterol. Too much cholesterol in the blood can lead to coronary artery disease.

questions.question: When should I see a doctor about back pain?
questions.reference: Most back pain goes away on its own, but if it is severe or does not improve after three days, you should call your health care provider. Staying in bed for more than one or two days can make it worse.

questions.question: What are the common types of arthritis?
questions.reference: Common types include osteoarthritis, the most common type, often related to aging or injury, and autoimmune arthritis, which happens when the immune system attacks the body. Most types cause joint pain and swelling, and treatment depends on the type.

questions.question: How is measles prevented and is there a treatment?
questions.reference: There is no treatment for measles, but the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine can prevent it. Measles is a viral infection that spreads easily and causes a blotchy red rash, fever, cough, runny nose and pink eye. German measles (rubella) is a different illness.

questions.question: What are the symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome?
questions.reference: Numbness, tingling or burning in the fingers, especially the thumb, index and middle fingers, often in both hands. Early on it starts slowly in the dominant hand and happens at night if the wrists are bent during sleep; as it worsens there can be tingling, pain or weakness with activities like driving or holding a phone.

questions.question: Symptome von Diabetes?
questions.reference: Zu den Symptomen von Diabetes können starker Durst, starker Hunger, häufigeres Wasserlassen (auch nachts), Müdigkeit, verschwommenes Sehen, Taubheit oder Kribbeln in Füßen oder Händen, schlecht heilende Wunden und ungewollter Gewichtsverlust gehören. Typ-1-Symptome kommen meist schnell und können schwer sein; Typ-2-Symptome entwickeln sich oft langsam über Jahre und können so mild sein, dass man sie nicht bemerkt.

questions.question: Was ist Gicht?
questions.reference: Gicht ist eine häufige entzündliche Form der Arthritis. Sie verursacht Schmerzen, Schwellung und Rötung in einem oder mehreren Gelenken, meist als Anfall, der ein bis zwei Wochen dauert und dann abklingt; oft beginnt er im großen Zeh. Ursache ist zu viel Harnsäure im Körper, die in manchen Menschen nadelförmige Kristalle in den Gelenken bildet.

questions.question: Wie wird Bluthochdruck behandelt?
questions.reference: Bluthochdruck wird mit herzgesunden Lebensstiländerungen (z. B. gesunde Ernährung und Bewegung) und, wenn diese nicht ausreichen, mit Medikamenten behandelt. Gemeinsam mit dem Arzt oder der Ärztin wird ein Behandlungsplan erstellt; manchmal genügen Lebensstiländerungen allein.

questions.question: Was sind die Symptome einer Blasenentzündung?
questions.reference: Anzeichen einer Harnwegsinfektion sind Schmerzen oder Brennen beim Wasserlassen, Fieber, Müdigkeit oder Zittrigkeit, häufiger Harndrang, Druck im Unterbauch, übel riechender oder trüber bzw. rötlicher Urin und Schmerzen im Rücken oder in der Seite unterhalb der Rippen.

questions.question: Was ist Migräne?
questions.reference: Migräne ist eine wiederkehrende Form von Kopfschmerzen mit mäßigen bis starken, pochenden oder pulsierenden Schmerzen, oft auf einer Kopfseite. Weitere Symptome können Übelkeit und Schwäche sein, außerdem Empfindlichkeit gegenüber Licht und Geräuschen. Man nimmt eine genetische Ursache an; Auslöser wie Stress, Hormonschwankungen, grelles Licht, Lärm oder Schlafmangel sind individuell verschieden.
